Working notes: Inventory reorder task.

Demand pattern: observed daily sales 3,7,5,3,10,2,0,6,3. Average ~4.3/day, volatile, max 10. Stockouts occur when stock is 0 and no same-day arrival covers demand. Sold-out days signal lost sales/penalties.

Costs: day costs are usually modest when stock covers demand (0.00–1.50). Unmet demand is expensive: 7.50 when stock 2 vs sales 10; 5.00 when stock 0 and sold out. Avoid stockouts more than minimizing small holding/order costs.

Policy: target enough stock to cover lead-time demand plus buffer. Reorder when projected stock drops below roughly 8–10 units. If stock is 0 and no arrival today, order at least 7–10 units. If a large same-day/next-day arrival is already scheduled and covers expected demand, ordering 0 can be acceptable (e.g., stock 0 with 12 arriving). If stock is adequate and arrivals are coming, no order was fine.

Ops: morning counts have matched system when noted; cycle count scheduled end of month. New receiving temp noted repeatedly; no receiving discrepancies yet, but monitor.

Learned: do not wait until fully sold out; demand spikes to 10. Maintain buffer. Ordering after stockouts is reactive and costly. At Day 10, stock 0, ordered 7; reasonable given recent demand.

Working notes: Inventory reorder task.

Policy: prevent stockouts; do not wait until 0. Target 10–14 units of buffer. Reorder when projected stock before reliable arrival drops below ~10, or stock is <=4 with no same-day arrival. If stock is 0 and no same-day arrival, order at least 10, but expect today may still be costly because reactive ordering is late. If stock is 0 and same-day/first arrival is >=10, ordering 0 can be OK (Day20 cost 2.0). If stock is 0 and same-day arrival is only 4–7, order enough to reach ~14 (e.g., 7–10). If adequate stock and near-term arrivals cover demand, no order is fine.

Working notes: Inventory reorder task.

Demand: recent 14 sales vary 0–14; avg ~5–6/day, spikes to 10–14, zeros possible. Stockouts are costly. Days with stock 0/1 and no same-day arrival cost 11.5–24.5 even when ordering 10–14. Same-day arrival 10–14 often keeps cost low (0.6–5.0), but 10 may not cover a 14-unit spike.

Policy: prevent stockouts before they occur; reactive ordering after stock hits 0 is usually late. If stock is 0 or 1 and no same-day arrival, today’s cost is often unavoidable; order for future demand but expect lost sales. If stock is 0 and first arrival >=10, ordering 0 can be OK, but if recent demand spiked or first arrival is only 10, consider ordering extra for following days. Target buffer 14–20, not 10–14, because spikes reach 14. Reorder when projected stock before reliable arrival drops below ~14. If stock <=4 and no same-day arrival, order now for future. If stock 0 and no same-day arrival, order at least 14. If adequate same-day/near-term arrivals cover expected demand, no order is fine.

Policy: target buffer 14–20. If stock + reliable near-term arrivals cover expected demand, order 0. If stock >=14 and arrivals cover demand, no order. If stock <14 and no/weak arrivals, order to restore ~14–20. If stock 0 and no same-day/next arrival, order at least 14; if a 14-unit arrival is same-day/next, order 0 or small. Reactive ordering after stock hits 0 is usually late. Earlier stockout costs 11.5–24.5 when no same-day arrival; same-day 10–14 kept costs 0.6–5.0.
